cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: This cathedral stands on the soft lakebed of Lake Texcoco, so it has sunk unevenly and parts of it lean. In the 1990s engineers removed soil under the higher parts to even it out.

cards.headline: About this shoe-shine stand
cards.note: Bolear, shining shoes, is an old street trade in Mexico City. Many people return to the same bolero again and again, and chat while they sit up in the raised chair, so the stand is also a place for talk.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: A guajolota is a tamal tucked inside a bolillo, a crusty white roll. People in Mexico City eat it as a cheap, filling morning meal, often with a cup of warm, thick atole.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Pumas and América meet in the Clásico Capitalino, and families are often split between the two clubs. At the table, the argument can last longer than the match.

cards.headline: About this chocolate mill
cards.note: At a chocolate mill in Oaxaca, cacao is ground fresh with sugar and cinnamon, and often almonds. Each customer asks for the mix they like, and the paste is pressed into tablets to take home.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Oaxacan weavers dye rug wool with cochineal, a small insect living on nopal cactus. Dried and crushed, it gives a deep red; mixed with lemon or other plants, it gives other shades.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every 12 October, huge crowds walk the Virgin's image to her basilica. People call her la Generala. Families wait on the streets to see her pass, keeping a promise or a family habit.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The Clásico Tapatío pits Chivas against Atlas, Guadalajara's two big teams. In 2021 Atlas won the league title after waiting about seventy years, and many fans cried in the streets and in the cantinas.

cards.headline: About this bakery
cards.note: Birote salado has a hard crust and a dense, soft crumb. It is the traditional roll for a torta ahogada, a meat roll drowned in salsa, because it keeps its shape under the sauce.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People have café de olla, coffee brewed with cinnamon and piloncillo, with breakfast or an afternoon snack, alongside a concha or pan de nata. The sweet spice feels like home.

cards.headline: About this art centre
cards.note: This art centre was once a textile factory where cotton cloth was woven for decades. After it closed, the big halls became studios, galleries and design shops, with high ceilings and plenty of light.

cards.headline: About this market stall
cards.note: What makes a cemita a cemita is pápalo, a strong-tasting herb that is usually added fresh and raw. Some people love it and some ask for it on the side, so Lupe always asks how you like yours.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Puebla and Oaxaca both take great pride in their moles, and people from each place will happily argue that theirs is better. Oaxaca is known for having several different moles, while Puebla's is dark and rich.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every 5 May, the city holds a civic parade for its 1862 victory over a French force. The French took it the next year, yet locals still mark the day as their own history.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Real Talavera from Puebla and nearby Tlaxcala has an official designation of origin and is made by hand. So a cup at a Puebla café may sometimes be a small piece of local craftwork.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: A fonda is a small place, often run by a family, that serves the day's home cooking at a fair price. Many people eat there at midday, and many Mexicans say the best food is at the fonda.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: At a fonda, the comida corrida is a set lunch, usually served from about one to five. For one price you get soup, rice or pasta, a main dish with tortillas, and an agua fresca.

cards.headline: About this tlayuda grill
cards.note: Before corn becomes masa, it is soaked and cooked with cal, lime. The lime loosens the kernel's tough skin so the dough holds together for tlayudas. It also frees niacin, a B vitamin, and adds calcium.

rows.en: Pardon? How can I help you?
A polite way to say "pardon?" when someone calls you.
You say it to people who are eating.
I'm a chilango, I was born here.
Chilanga is the form for a woman.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: La comida is the main meal of the day, eaten in the middle of the afternoon. Afterwards, people often stay at the table for a long sobremesa.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Día de Muertos is celebrated with ofrendas and cempasúchil. Pan de muerto is one of the foods of the season.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many people eat standing up at a taco stand, a puesto de tacos. When you order, you can ask for "con todo", which means with everything.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: On the street, people give a tip to the franelero, the person who looks after the cars. It is a common custom in the city.

rows.en: A warm invitation to step inside.
Yes, dear. What can we get you?
A fond way to address customers.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The main meal of the day is eaten between two and four in the afternoon. In the fondas, many places serve comida corrida at that hour.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: When you walk into a place where someone is eating, people say buen provecho. It is a small courtesy to wish them a good meal.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Mezcal is sipped slowly, in small sips. It is served with orange and sal de gusano, a salt made with worm.

rows.en: It names the people of this city.
Literally it means wool. People use it for money.
Can you pass me the salt?
A polite way to ask someone to say it again.
A cheerful way to say something is great.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many people have a set lunch in the afternoon, usually between 2 and 4 pm. It is called the comida corrida.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People say buen provecho to others who are eating. It is a common custom, and it wishes them a good meal.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Friends and family greet each other with a kiss on the cheek. Shop owners also greet customers with a buenos días or buenas tardes as they walk in.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: On weekends, mariachi music is played in the plazas. It is a part of how people spend their free time outdoors.

rows.en: Said to people eating as you come or go.
Pardon? I didn't quite catch that.
A polite way to ask someone to repeat.
Excuse me, I'm going to pass.
Said when you need to get past.
Come in, what can we get you?
A warm way to welcome someone in.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In a shop or a fonda, people greet everyone with buenas tardes before asking for anything. The greeting comes first, before the order or the question.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Comida corrida is the main meal of the day. It is eaten in the afternoon, usually around 2 pm.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In the evening, people take a paseo around the Jardín. Families, couples and mariachis are all out for it.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every September, La Alborada lights up the sky with fireworks. The celebration honours San Miguel Arcángel.

rows.en: A polite way to say you didn't catch something.
Both are friendly ways to address a stranger.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The main meal, la comida, is eaten between 2 and 4 pm. Many people have a menú del día at a fonda, followed by a long sobremesa at the table.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: When people enter a small shop, they greet the owner with "buenas tardes".

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Chiles en nogada are a seasonal dish, eaten in August and September. They come in the colours of the Mexican flag.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Small purchases are made with coins and small bills. Shops often cannot change large ones.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: For Día de Muertos, families gather around altars with pan de muerto and marigolds.

rows.en: I like wandering the alleys at night.
Note: Here the streets are alleys and tunnels, so wandering them comes naturally.
Pardon? I didn't hear you well.
Note: A polite way to ask someone to say it again.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Evenings are for callejoneadas with the estudiantinas. The name comes from callejonear, to wander the alleys.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People get around through tunnels under the city, by bus, taxi or on foot. The streets are alleys and tunnels, so walking is the way to go everywhere.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: For the Day of the Dead, people build altars and visit the cemetery. In Spanish it is called el Día de Muertos.

rows.en: I'm a jarocho, from the port.
What can I give you, love?
A vendor may call anyone this.
It is a casual word for something you like.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: At the Café de la Parroquia, people tap their glass with a spoon to ask for milk.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Fandangos are gatherings with son jarocho music. Anyone can sing a verse.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People say buen provecho to those who are eating. It is a polite thing to say.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The Carnival of Veracruz takes place before Lent. It includes parades on the malecón.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Vuelve a la vida is a seafood cocktail. Its name means "come back to life."

rows.en: Note: People lovingly call Vasco de Quiroga "Tata Vasco."

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: On Janitzio, people keep an all-night vigil for the Day of the Dead.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The Danza de los Viejitos is danced at fiestas.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Each town around the lake has its own craft. The tradition goes back to Tata Vasco.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Market day is held around the Plaza Chica.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People say buen provecho to those who are eating.

rows.en: Bomba! A call before a verse.
Note: At a vaquería, it comes before a rhyming verse.
the last drop left in a glass
Only the last drop is left.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: A local custom is wearing white. Men wear the guayabera, and women wear the hipil or the terno.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People here use Maya words in everyday Spanish. For example, ¡Ma’alob! means “fine” in Maya.

rows.en: Coleto is for a man, coleta for a woman.
Some families here speak Tsotsil at home.
Chulo goes with masculine words, chula with feminine ones.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many families here speak Tsotsil or Tseltal at home. In town, people speak Spanish.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Each barrio, or neighborhood, has its own church and its own saint's day.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In the evening, marimba music plays in the plaza.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In December, torch runners carry fire for the Virgin of Guadalupe.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Ask before you take anyone's photo. And never take one inside the church at Chamula.

rows.en: Shall we go to the beach?
Shall we go to La Revu?
Yes, let's go to La Revu.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many people cross to the United States to work, study or shop. Before they go, they check the wait at the border crossing, la línea.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In Plaza Santa Cecilia, you can hire musicians by the song. You pick a song, and they play it for you.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People here pay in pesos or in dollars. Both are part of everyday life, so it helps to know how to use either.

rows.en: Excuse me, can you help me?
You can say it politely to anyone.

cards.headline: Two ways to say the United States

rows.text: Mi tío vive en el norte.
rows.en: My uncle lives in the United States.

cards.headline: A word for the pink stone

rows.text: La cantera es una piedra rosa.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In a callejoneada, people walk the alleys behind a tamborazo. A donkey goes along carrying the mezcal.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In December, relatives come home from the United States. People here call that country el norte or el otro lado.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Mezcal is drunk neat, with nothing mixed in, and slowly.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Queso de tuna is a sweet, not a cheese. It is made from cactus fruit, which is called tuna.

rows.en: Are you coming to the carne asada?
My uncle is very tight with money.

rows.text: Es muy codo con el dinero.
rows.en: He's very tight with his money.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: On weekends, Monterrey families gather for carne asada. It is a big get-together with the whole family, and the neighbours come too.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The Clásico Regio is the big match between Rayados and Tigres, the two teams of Monterrey. It is a famous local rivalry.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: When the heat breaks, people go out to walk the Paseo Santa Lucía. It is a favourite way to enjoy the cooler hours.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Glorias are a sweet made from milk and pecans. They come from Linares, in Nuevo León.

rows.en: Shall we go to the beach?

rows.text: Los plebes están en la playa.
rows.en: The kids are at the beach.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Carnival is held in the week before Lent. There are parades on the malecón, the seaside promenade.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Winter here is baseball season. The team people go out to watch is the Venados.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Café de olla is made in a clay pot with cinnamon and piloncillo, which is unrefined cane sugar. Chiapas and Veracruz are among the states that grow Mexico's coffee.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: This park was laid out in the 1920s on the site of a racetrack. Avenida Amsterdam still follows the oval of the old track around it.

cards.headline: About this cantina
cards.note: The cantina opened in 1895; its carved wooden bar, tall mirrors and ornate ceiling are from then. A bullet hole in the ceiling is said to be Pancho Villa's, though nobody can prove it.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This is the oldest public park in the Americas, laid out in 1592 under Viceroy Luis de Velasco. It is named for its álamos, the poplar trees.

cards.headline: About this cathedral
cards.note: Building went on from 1573 to the early 1800s, so it mixes Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical styles. It stands on soft lake-bed clay and has sunk unevenly over time. Plumb lines hang inside.

cards.headline: About this churrería
cards.note: This churrería has been open day and night since 1935. The hot chocolate comes light, called mexicano, or thick, called español.

cards.headline: About this market stall
cards.note: Here a quesadilla doesn't automatically come with cheese; it's 'con queso' only if asked. Huitlacoche, a favorite filling, is a prized fungus that grows on corn.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: A cocina económica serves the comida corrida: one price for soup, rice, a guisado and agua de jamaica. The menu is written on the chalkboard each morning.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: A tlayuda is a large, crisp corn tortilla spread with asiento (pork lard), beans and quesillo. Tasajo and cecina enchilada are grilled over charcoal, so smoke fills the aisle.

cards.headline: About this mezcalería
cards.note: Mezcal is sipped slowly from small copitas, with orange slices and sal de gusano: ground dried agave worm with salt and chile. Espadín is the agave poured most often.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Café de olla is coffee brewed in a clay pot with cinnamon and piloncillo. Here it is served with pan de yema.

cards.headline: About this market stall
cards.note: A little friendly haggling is normal in the market. Sellers add the pilón, a little extra for the customer.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: This is the land of seven moles: negro, coloradito, amarillo, rojo, verde, chichilo and manchamanteles. Mole negro gets its dark color from chiles chilhuacles and toasted seeds, and takes days to make.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: When the barrio holds a fiesta, bells and cohetes announce it from the morning. Then a calenda procession, with marmotas and giant puppets, winds through the cobbled streets.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Monte Albán is a Zapotec city built on a levelled mountaintop more than two thousand years ago. Its Gran Plaza is a vast levelled square with temples along its sides.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: The Mercado San Juan de Dios, also called Mercado Libertad, is one of the largest indoor markets in Latin America. Next to it, carts sell tejuino, a cold Jalisco drink of fermented corn masa and piloncillo.

cards.headline: About this cantina
cards.note: In a traditional cantina, tequila comes in a small caballito, often with sangrita, a Jalisco invention, on the side. Botanas arrive at the table to share. Tequila is made from blue agave in Jalisco.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Colonia Americana was built in the early 20th century, and its houses copy American and European styles, hence the name. Its main street, Avenida Chapultepec, has a wide tree-lined walkway down the middle.

cards.headline: About this bakery
cards.note: Guadalajara is known for birote salado, a crusty sourdough roll. It is the only bread that works for tortas ahogadas, so people come early before it sells out.

cards.headline: About this workshop
cards.note: Tlaquepaque is known for its pottery, and its pedestrian Calle Independencia is lined with galleries and craft shops. Barro bruñido is a local style: the clay is polished by hand with a smooth stone.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Hospicio Cabañas was an orphanage. Orozco's Man of Fire is in its dome. Orozco painted his murals with one hand; he lost the left when he was young.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Mariachi comes from Jalisco. A group has violins, trumpets, a guitarrón and a vihuela, and the players wear the charro suit. Groups wait in the plaza to be hired for a song.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: The market is named after Ignacio Ramírez, "El Nigromante", born in this town. Orange cempasúchil marigolds go first on Día de Muertos altars; their color and scent are said to guide the dead home.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: In the evening the Jardín Allende fills for the paseo, with families, couples and mariachis. Taxis wait by it to take people along the cobbled streets of the Centro.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Parroquia's pink-stone neo-Gothic façade was designed in the late 1800s by Zeferino Gutiérrez, a local self-taught builder. The church faces the Jardín, the town's main square.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Café de olla is brewed in a clay pot with piloncillo and cinnamon. A concha or a pan de nata goes with it.

cards.headline: About this art centre
cards.note: Fábrica La Aurora was a textile mill until it closed in the 1990s. It is now an art and design centre of studios and galleries, and visitors can walk in and look around.

cards.headline: About this taquería
cards.note: For tacos al pastor, the pork turns on a vertical spit called a trompo, with a pineapple on top. The method comes from the shawarma brought to Mexico by Lebanese immigrants.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Ignacio Allende was born in 1769 in this house on the Jardín, now a museum. He and Father Hidalgo began the fight for independence in 1810. The town added his name in 1826.

cards.headline: About this sweet shop
cards.note: Calle 6 Oriente is nicknamed the "Calle de los Dulces". People buy sweets there to take home as gifts, like camote, a sweet-potato candy, and tortitas de Santa Clara, made of pumpkin-seed paste.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: Chiles en nogada come in late summer, when walnuts and pomegranates are fresh. Their green, white and red match the Mexican flag.

cards.headline: About this library
cards.note: The Biblioteca Palafoxiana began in 1646, when Bishop Juan de Palafox gave his books to the seminary on condition that anyone could read them. Poblanos call it the first public library in the Americas.

cards.headline: About this cantina
cards.note: La Pasita is well known for its pasita, a raisin liqueur. It is served in a small glass with a raisin, a bit of cheese and a toothpick.

cards.headline: About this taquería
cards.note: Tacos árabes are the favorite late-night street food in Puebla, so taquerías like this one are busiest at night.

cards.headline: About this neighborhood
cards.note: Xanenetla is one of the oldest barrios of Puebla. Its murals cover the neighbours' own house fronts, painted together with the people who live behind them.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The historic center around the Jardín del Carmen is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Many church domes and façades here are covered in Talavera tile.

cards.headline: About this street
cards.note: Guanajuato sits in a narrow ravine. After floods, the river was diverted, and its old bed under the stone bridges became tunnels. Today they carry most of the city's traffic.

cards.headline: About this theatre
cards.note: The Teatro Juárez was opened in 1903 by President Porfirio Díaz. Inside, it is all red velvet and gilded Moorish decoration.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This was a grain store where the Spanish took refuge in September 1810, in the first great battle of the War of Independence. Today it is a regional museum.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: In the late 1700s the Valenciana mine next door was one of the world's richest silver mines. The Count of Valenciana built this church, with carved altars covered in gold.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: The house dish is enchiladas mineras: tortillas in guajillo chile sauce, filled with cheese and onion, topped with fried potatoes and carrots. Said to be the miners' food, cheap and filling.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: This café on the malecón goes back to the early 1800s. For a lechero, tap your glass of strong coffee with a spoon and a waiter pours hot milk from high up.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Couples dance danzón here in the open air several evenings a week, to a live band. It came from Cuba in the late 1800s and became the city's own: slow, elegant, danced close.

cards.headline: About this fortress
cards.note: Built by the Spanish on an island from the sixteenth century, this fortress was the last place in Mexico held by Spanish troops, until 1825. Later it was a feared prison.

cards.headline: About this bastion
cards.note: This bastion is all that is left of the city walls, built in the seventeenth century against pirates after raids like the one in 1683. The rest was pulled down as the city grew.

cards.headline: About this stall
cards.note: Picadas are the breakfast of the port: thick rounds of corn dough with the edges pinched up, topped with red or green salsa, cheese and onion. Stalls open early for the dockworkers.

cards.headline: About this cemetery
cards.note: On the night of 1 November, Purépecha families of the island sit up all night among the graves with candles, cempasúchil flowers, bread and the dead person's favourite food, welcoming the returning souls.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This is one of the largest plazas in Mexico, named for Vasco de Quiroga, still called Tata Vasco. He is credited with giving each Purépecha lake town its own craft; many still do.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: Here the food is from the lake: sopa tarasca, a bean and tomato soup; corundas, triangular tamales in corn leaf; and, rarely now, pescado blanco, a small white fish. Dessert is nieve de pasta.

cards.headline: About this workshop
cards.note: This eighteenth-century convent now holds artisans' workshops where maque, lacquerware, is made. The lacquer is often black, painted with flowers and birds and outlined in fine gold leaf. The craft predates the Spanish.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: This was the capital of the Purépecha kingdom before the Spanish. Its five yácatas are pyramids with a round and a rectangular part, unlike any others in Mexico. The name means place of the hummingbirds.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Since the 1960s, this park has held a weekly evening serenata of trova yucateca: romantic songs for two guitars and voices, with boleros, claves and bambucos.

cards.headline: About this street
cards.note: This boulevard was laid out at the end of the nineteenth century on the model of the Paris boulevards. Its mansions were built with henequen money; some are now museums, banks and hotels.

cards.headline: About this street-food stand
cards.note: Cochinita pibil is pork marinated in achiote and sour orange juice, wrapped in banana leaves and cooked slowly in a pib, a pit oven in the ground. Pib is a Maya word.

cards.headline: About this street-food stand
cards.note: Lebanese families settled in Yucatán at the end of the nineteenth century, and their food became Yucatecan. The kibi, from Arab kibbeh, is fried ground meat and wheat, eaten with pickled red onion and habanero.

cards.headline: About this workshop
cards.note: Many Yucatecans sleep in a hammock rather than a bed, because it is cooler in the heat, and every house has hooks in the walls. A good hammock takes weeks to weave.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Inside the church of San Juan Chamula there are no pews and no regular Mass. Pine needles cover the floor, and families kneel among candles to pray in Tsotsil. Photographs are strictly forbidden.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Each town in the highlands has its own clothes. In Zinacantán they are covered in embroidered flowers, because the town grows flowers in greenhouses. One blouse can take a month to make.

cards.headline: About this comedor
cards.note: A Chiapas comedor makes tamales de chipilín, with a green herb in the dough; de bola, filled with pork, prunes and raisins; and de hoja de plátano, wrapped in banana leaf.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Chiapas grows more coffee than any other Mexican state, mostly on small mountain plots of Indigenous families, in the shade of taller trees. Cherries are picked red by hand, about November to March.

cards.headline: About this cathedral
cards.note: Bartolomé de las Casas came here as bishop in 1545 and spent his life denouncing the Spanish treatment of Indigenous people. The city carries his name.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: The Caesar salad was born here in the 1920s, when Americans crossed the border to drink during Prohibition. The story goes that Caesar Cardini made it in 1924 from what was left in the kitchen.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: This has been the traditional market since the 1950s. Stalls sell what Mixtec families from Oaxaca miss, like chile pasilla, chapulines and quesillo, beside Baja California cheese and dates.

cards.headline: About this taquería
cards.note: The local taco is carne asada: beef grilled over mesquite charcoal, chopped, on a corn tortilla with onion, cilantro, salsa and guacamole. The local name for al pastor is adobada.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The casino and hotel opened in 1928, when alcohol and gambling were banned in the United States, and Hollywood crossed the border to play. In 1935 casinos were banned and it became a school.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This plaza is named for Santa Cecilia, patron saint of musicians. People come to hire a group by the song or by the hour, for a birthday, a serenade or a funeral.

cards.headline: About this cathedral
cards.note: Zacatecas is built of cantera rosa, a soft pink stone quarried nearby that hardens in the air. The cathedral's front, finished in the mid-1700s, is carved like lace, paid for by silver.

cards.headline: About this hill
cards.note: In 1914 Pancho Villa's División del Norte took this hill and the city from the federal army, in one of the Revolution's bloodiest battles. Three bronze horsemen outside show Villa, Ángeles and Natera.

cards.headline: About this cable car
cards.note: The cable car crosses the centre, from Cerro del Grillo to Cerro de la Bufa. From the cabin you see a city squeezed into a ravine between hills full of silver.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: The museum holds thousands of Mexican masks, one of the largest collections in the world: devils, jaguars, Moors and Christians, carved for village dances. It stands in the ruins of a sixteenth-century convent.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: Gorditas are thick corn tortillas cooked on the comal, split and filled with stew. People here eat them at any hour. The classic filling is asado de boda, pork in dark red chile sauce.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Macroplaza is one of the largest plazas in the world. Whole blocks of the old centre were knocked down to build it in the early 1980s.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Parque Fundidora was a steelworks, founded in 1900 as the first big one in Latin America. It closed in 1986, and blast furnace number three is now a museum of steel.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: Cabrito is the dish of Nuevo León: a milk-fed kid goat, opened flat on an iron stake and cooked slowly for hours beside mesquite embers, never over the flame.

cards.headline: About this taco stand
cards.note: Tacos mañaneros are small breakfast tacos in flour tortillas, filled with stews. Machacado is beef dried in the sun and pounded, then scrambled with egg.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: The Palacio del Obispado, the bishop's palace built in the 1780s, is the oldest large building in the city. In September 1846 the US army attacked, and this hill was among the last positions to fall.

cards.headline: About this theatre
cards.note: The theatre opened in 1874. After a hurricane it became a ruin with trees inside, until the city restored it in 1992. Now it has opera, ballet and an autumn festival.

cards.headline: About this street market
cards.note: The changueras, all women, have sold shrimp from tubs of ice on this street for generations. The whole city buys here, by the kilo and by size, for ceviche, aguachile or the grill.

cards.headline: About this cathedral
cards.note: Each of the cathedral's twenty-eight stained-glass windows has a six-pointed star. People say it thanks a Jewish family of the port who gave money to finish the building.

cards.headline: About this lighthouse
cards.note: The lighthouse stands about 150 metres above the sea on a hill that was once an island, one of the highest lighthouses in the world. From the top you see the whole port.

cards.headline: About this seafood cart
cards.note: Seafood here is mostly for morning and midday, so carts close in the afternoon. Small boats land their catch each morning at the fishermen's beach. Carts serve ceviche, aguachile and oysters.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Parque México is laid out in an oval because it follows the track of the old Hipódromo de la Condesa, a horse racing course. Today it is known for its Art Deco style and its dog walkers.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The cathedral took about 250 years to build, from 1573 to 1813, so it mixes several styles. It stands on the soft ground of the old lake bed, and it has sunk unevenly over time.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Alameda dates from 1592, which makes it one of the oldest public parks in the Americas. Its name comes from álamo, the Spanish word for poplar, the trees first planted here.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Diego Rivera began painting the grand staircase murals in 1929. They tell the history of Mexico, from the pre-Hispanic world through the Spanish conquest to the twentieth century.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: A fountain of coyotes stands in this garden, which suits the neighbourhood. The name Coyoacán comes from Nahuatl and is usually translated as "place of coyotes."

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This park is named for Cassiano Conzatti, an Italian-born botanist who studied the plants of Oaxaca and lived in the region for many years. It is a shaded green space in the city center.

cards.headline: About this garden
cards.note: It grows plants from across Oaxaca, especially cacti, on the grounds of the former Santo Domingo monastery. It opened in the late 1990s, and you visit it on a guided tour.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This is the main square of the city, with the cathedral and the government palace on its sides and arcades full of cafés. Families and friends meet here, and music often plays.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Zapotecs founded Monte Albán around 500 BC on a flattened mountaintop above the valley. It was one of the first great cities of Mesoamerica and a Zapotec capital for centuries.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Hospicio Cabañas began as a shelter for orphans and the poor. Its chapel is covered in murals by José Clemente Orozco, including the famous Man of Fire in the dome. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Mariachi bands in charro suits wait here to be hired, and you can ask them to play a song. Mariachi music was born in Jalisco, the state whose capital is Guadalajara.

cards.headline: About this market stall
cards.note: This stall is in the Mercado Ignacio Ramírez, named for the writer and liberal thinker born in San Miguel in 1818. He was known by his pen name, El Nigromante.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Jardín is the town's main square. Its laurel trees are trimmed into neat shapes, and the Parroquia stands on one side. Locals sit here to talk and pass the time.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Parroquia's pink stone, Gothic-style façade dates from the late 1800s. It was designed by a local mason, Zeferino Gutiérrez, and it is now the symbol of San Miguel.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This house is where Ignacio Allende was born in 1769. He became a leader of Mexico's fight for independence, and the town was renamed in his honor.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: El Mirador is a lookout on a hill above the town. From here you can see the rooftops of the center and the spires of the Parroquia.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Santo Domingo was built by Dominican friars. Its Rosary Chapel, finished in 1690, is covered in gold leaf and counts among the finest works of Mexican Baroque.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Zócalo is Puebla's main square. The cathedral stands on one side, and arcades with cafés and restaurants line the others. Locals have gathered here for centuries.

cards.headline: About this library
cards.note: Bishop Juan de Palafox founded this library in 1646 by donating his own books. It is often called the first public library in the Americas, and UNESCO lists it in its Memory of the World register.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This small triangular garden is the social heart of the city. Its laurel trees are trimmed into neat rounded shapes, and cafés and restaurants line its edges, with a bandstand where people gather for music.

cards.headline: About this theater
cards.note: The Teatro Juárez opened in 1903, with President Porfirio Díaz at the ceremony. Today it is one of the main venues of the Festival Internacional Cervantino, held every year.

cards.headline: About this monument
cards.note: This statue honors El Pípila, the miner said to have set fire to the Alhóndiga door in 1810, during the fight for independence. He holds a torch above the city, and the view is great.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: The Alhóndiga was built as a grain storehouse. In 1810 it became the site of the first major battle of the War of Independence. Today it is a museum of regional history.

cards.headline: About this university
cards.note: The University of Guanajuato traces its roots to a school founded in 1732. Its main building is famous for the wide white staircase that climbs up from the street.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: This church was paid for by the owner of the Valenciana silver mine and finished in 1788. It is famous for its ornate Churrigueresque style and its golden altarpieces.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This house is where the painter Diego Rivera was born in 1886. Now a museum, it shows works by the artist along with furnishings from the family home.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Around this plaza stand the Palacio Municipal and the Parroquia de la Asunción, with cafés under the arcades. Musicians, from marimba players to son jarocho groups, often play here in the evening.

cards.headline: About this fortress
cards.note: This fortress sits on an island in the harbor and guarded the port from the 1500s. It later served as a prison. Spanish troops held it until 1825, years after Mexican independence.

cards.headline: About this bulwark
cards.note: This is the only surviving bulwark of the walls once built around the city to defend it against pirates. Construction began in the 1600s. Today visitors can go inside.

cards.headline: About this cemetery
cards.note: On the night of Día de Muertos, families on the island keep a candlelit vigil at the graves. They bring marigolds, food and music for their dead, and many visitors cross the lake by boat to watch.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This wide plaza is named for Vasco de Quiroga, the 16th-century bishop still honored for organizing Purépecha villages around different crafts. Many of those crafts are still made today. His statue stands in the center.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: This basilica holds the Virgin of Health, an image made by Purépecha artisans from corn-cane paste, which is very light. Pilgrims have come to pray before her for centuries.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The yácatas are the stone temple platforms of the Purépecha, whose capital stood here. Unlike most Mexican pyramids, they combine rounded and rectangular forms, and they look out over the lake.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Arcades line this plaza, where stagecoaches once stopped. Today it's known for the serenata, an open-air evening of Yucatecan music, poetry and dance.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Palacio de Gobierno houses the state government of Yucatán. Inside, murals by Fernando Castro Pacheco tell the story of the Maya and of Yucatán, and visitors can walk in to see them.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Opened in 2012, this museum is dedicated to Maya civilization, from ancient times to today. Its building is inspired by the ceiba, the sacred tree of the Maya.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Built in 1748, this chapel stood on the old road to Campeche. Travelers leaving the city stopped here to pray for a safe journey.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Inside there are no pews. Pine needles cover the floor, and thousands of candles burn. Tsotsil Maya families pray in their own language, mixing Catholic and Maya traditions. Photos are not allowed inside.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Beside the church of Santo Domingo, Tsotsil and Tseltal Maya artisans sell hand-woven and embroidered textiles, along with amber jewelry. Chiapas is well known for its amber.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The main square is named for the date the city was founded: 31 March 1528. The cathedral and the town hall stand around it, and people gather here all day.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The church stands on a small hill at the end of the street Real de Guadalupe, up a flight of steps. Each 12 December, people celebrate the Virgin of Guadalupe here.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Na Bolom means "House of the Jaguar" in Tsotsil. It was the home of Frans Blom, a Danish archaeologist, and Gertrude Duby-Blom, a photographer who worked with the Lacandon Maya.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The cathedral stands on the north side of the main plaza. Its ochre and red front is carved in the baroque style, and it is one of the best-known sights of the city.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Mariachi musicians gather in this small plaza, ready to be hired to play. Santa Cecilia, the plaza's namesake, is the patron saint of musicians.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: This tower is what remains of the Agua Caliente resort and casino, which opened in 1928 and drew Hollywood stars. Mexico banned gambling in 1935, and the casino closed.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The cathedral is built of pink quarry stone and was raised in the 1700s. Its richly carved front is considered one of the finest examples of Mexican Baroque.

cards.headline: About this hill
cards.note: La Bufa is the rocky hill above the city. In 1914 Pancho Villa's army won the Battle of Zacatecas here, and a monument on the hill recalls that victory.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: The museum stands in the ruins of an old Franciscan convent. It holds thousands of Mexican masks, collected by the painter Rafael Coronel, who was Diego Rivera's son-in-law.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Plaza de Armas is the heart of the historic center. The cathedral stands on one side and the Palacio de Gobierno on another. UNESCO lists the center as World Heritage.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Macroplaza is one of the largest city squares in the world, opened in the 1980s. Its landmark is the Faro del Comercio, an orange tower that shines a green laser across the sky at night.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Horno 3 is a giant blast furnace from the Fundidora steel foundry, which closed in 1986. The foundry grounds became a public park, and today the furnace is a museum about making steel.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Built in the late 1700s as a bishop's palace on a hilltop, it later served as a fort when U.S. troops attacked in 1846. Today it is a museum of regional history.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This small plaza is named for Juan N. Machado, a 19th-century businessman. Today it is the heart of the old town's evenings, with open-air cafés and restaurants beside the Teatro Ángela Peralta.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: This theatre opened in 1874 and was later named for the opera singer Ángela Peralta, "the Mexican Nightingale." She sang here in 1883 and died of yellow fever in Mazatlán that year.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: El Faro stands on Cerro del Crestón and is often called one of the highest natural lighthouses in the world. Reaching it means a steep walk up the hill.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Built in the second half of the 1800s, this cathedral is known for its two tall yellow towers and its mix of architectural styles. It is still an active place of worship.

I arrived the day before yesterday.
Getting past someone, or calling them over:
Excuse me, ma'am: let me pass.
Excuse me, ma'am: I need your attention.
It's a hundred and twenty pesos.
Mexico City: what people call it

Mérida: thank you, in Yucatec Maya
Guadalajara: a roll drowned in chile sauce
Puebla: a sandwich on a sesame roll
Oaxaca: one of its seven moles

cards.headline: Two places: a cold corn drink

rows.en: Oaxaca: cold drink of corn and cacao
Tijuana: where this salad was invented
Mazatlán: raw shrimp in chile and lime
Mexico City: a tamal inside a roll
